text: Good evening, neighbours. One of my lads is camped under the Wall right where Clark's fields meet Rich's, and the other's on a boat off the coast, just about where Silke's silk meets Paddy's rice. No tax from me, Reina. Collect it yourself if you like, I'll have the kettle on.
Rob stands W1 on G11, on the strip below the Wall where Provinces 2 and 3 meet, and W2 on Q26, in the sea off Provinces 5 and 6. He refuses to pay the crown's tax.

The Mandate comes from Heaven, so the crown will read Heaven's book itself. I'll shuffle the deck, turn the cards and keep the count, and nobody will need to wonder whose hand turned them. The first harvest will be a full one, so sharpen your sickles. The walls won't build themselves.
Reina will read the I Ching herself, unpaid, and shuffles the deck.

Your Majesty, what a gracious thing, reading Heaven's book with your own hands. Nobody at this table could doubt a count you keep. Silke, Paddy, my dears, it's the customary five each, the smallest rent in the empire, and the Pile pays out the moment the sickles are in. And Rob, keep your kettle, and keep your boys off my side of the Wall.
Rich asks Silke and Paddy for the minimum rent: each pays him 5.

Half the harvest, friends. The fields will never be fuller than they are tonight, and an empire that waits for lean years to build will never build at all. The Summer Palace goes up this year, and the Wall and the Canal start from it. Clark, collect it cleanly and you'll have your five at year's end. Rob, keep your kettle. The crown doesn't knock on tents.

Reina declares a tax of 50% on the first harvest: 30 each from Clark, Rich, Silke and Paddy, 120 in all; Rob refuses his. The crown will build the Summer Palace (20 from the reserve) and pay Clark 5 at the year's end.

Thirty from each of us, a hundred and twenty to the crown, counted twice and written down once. Majesty, it's in the ledger: fifty percent in the first year, and the Summer Palace before a single stone of the Wall. And Rob, I've noted your refusal too, with the date. A warlord the crown can't tax is a warlord the crown can't control, and that's a page in my book now.
Clark collects 30 each from himself, Rich, Silke and Paddy: 120 to the crown. Rob refuses his. Reina builds the Summer Palace on G20, 20 from the reserve.

The Customs House starts at three, friends. It's an honest house and it keeps honest books. As for the rest, I'll bid like a clerk, small and steady. Rich, you already own the land under us all, so you don't need the jar and the bowl as well. I'll be writing down who bids against whom.

Majesty, a palace first. Very wise, a crown ought to have a roof before it has a wall. My rent's in, Silke, Paddy, thank you both, and the Harvest Pile is safe with me. As for tonight's trinkets, I'll bid like a gentleman: modestly, and I'll pay on the nail. And my deeds go no lower than three. Land is land.

Let's count it out loud, shall we? Thirty to the crown, five to Rich, and the crown sits on a hundred and sixty while I sit on twenty-five. So I'll bid like a woman with twenty-five, and anyone who wants to run these prices up is just feeding the Pile. My Dragon Jar starts at three, and it's worth every grain.

Well, I paid my thirty and my five and I've twenty-five left to my name, so I won't be running anyone's prices up tonight. I'll put in a fair bid on each piece and no more. And my Bowl goes up at two. It's a plain thing, and I'd rather it went to a good table than sat in my kitchen.

Go on, bid, all of you. Buy your pretty jars and bowls and scrolls and put them out on the board where I can see them. I don't need to own a thing, friends. I only need to know where you've put it. And Clark, write this in your book too: the Warlord kept his sixty, and the crown spent twenty on a summer house nine rounds from my tent.

The auctions: Rich buys Clark's Customs House for 7 over Silke's and Paddy's 6. Clark buys Rich's Land Deed Scroll for 6 (Paddy also bid 6; a tie goes by seat order), Silke's Dragon Jar for 7 over Rich's and Paddy's 6, and Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 7 over Rich's and Silke's 6. Rob passes every lot. Clark now holds a complete set: Land Deed, Dragon Jar and Wooden Bowl.

A scroll, a jar and a bowl, all in the Official's keeping and all paid for on the nail. Rob, since you asked so nicely, they're at the back of my province, behind the clerks, the granary and a great deal of paperwork. And Rich, the Customs House is yours. Try to keep honest books in it.

A Customs House! Thank you, Clark. Seven grain, and a quarter of it back in your pocket, so we're practically partners. I'll keep it well back from the Wall. No need to tempt our friend in the tent. And Clark, a full set in your first year. Congratulations. I'm sure you'll be writing down who you mean to replace with it.
Clark places the Land Deed on J14, the Dragon Jar on J16 and the Wooden Bowl on I15; Rich places the Customs House on L10.

Clark, you can stack paperwork as high as the Wall and I'll still read it. Here's five for your river toll, and I'm taking five back for the walk. We'll call that our first transaction. Silke, sorry, love, the sea air makes me peckish. That's five off the coast, and nobody in this province ordered it except me.

Rob marches: W1 crosses the north river onto H12 in Province 2 (a 5 toll to Clark, and 5 raided from him); W2 comes ashore on P25, raiding 5 from Silke. At the year's end Reina pays Clark 5 as the Official.

Spring Floods. Heaven waters the land generously. In some places, far too generously." Provinces 1, 3, 6 and 7 have a good harvest. Provinces 2, 4, 5 and 8 have a bad one. The population holds at 100 million, times one, so read your first row. And yes, Heaven was kind to the crown's own province. Clark, Silke, I'm sorry about the water, but the empire still has to be built.

The pile pays out, friends, and gladly: Your Majesty forty, Clark ten, Silke ten, Paddy sixty, and sixty to your humble servant, since the floods were so kind to Province 3. Rent stays at the customary five each. I won't squeeze a flooded field, Silke, a landlord's only as good as his tenants' goodwill. I do hope the crown remembers the flooded provinces when the tax comes round, Your Majesty. Heaven has already taken its share there.

Fifty percent again, the same rate for every province, flooded or not. Heaven takes its share, Rich, and the crown takes its own. The Winter Palace goes up this year, and it opens the way for the southern canals. Clark, your five, as before.

Reina declares a tax of 50% again: Clark owes 5, Rich 30, Silke 5 and Paddy 30, 70 in all; Rob's income is nil. The crown will build the Winter Palace, all 20 from the reserve, and pay Clark 5 at the year's end.

Storyteller's tip, to Silke, said to the whole table: a revolt can be called at any step, by anyone, the Warlord included (Section 16). It needs its caller and two others agreeing on a cause, and the board card lists the causes. Once it's called with two agreeing, play stops until it stands or is dropped. The Emperor may answer it, and it stands only if the caller and two others still back it. One called now, before the tax is paid, voids this year's tax. Under Chaos nobody pays tax, salaries or works, and nobody can buy new land. The harvest, the rent, the auctions and the Warlord carry on. The reserve is sealed: nobody spends it, and it passes whole to whoever is acclaimed. The throne then goes only by acclamation. Anyone but the deposed Emperor may claim it, a peasant or the Warlord included, and the claimants are counted on grain in hand, soldiers on the board and friends.

Fifty percent in Year 1, Your Majesty, and fifty percent again on a flooded field. Two years running is a pattern, and patterns are what I write down. I'll collect if I'm asked to collect. But if anyone at this table names excessive tax as a cause, they'll find my name beside theirs, and I'll bring the ledger to prove it.

Your Majesty, I've praised this crown every year and I meant it. But fifty in the hundred, two years running, on drowned fields the same as dry ones? That isn't Heaven's share. If anyone at this table says the tax is too heavy, they'll have Richard Baron's name beside theirs. And once I give my name, I don't take it back.

Fifty percent last year, fifty percent this year, and fifty percent of a flooded field. I paid thirty last spring and got a palace I'll never see the inside of. Your Majesty, that's not a tax, that's a habit. I'm calling it: the taxes are consistently excessive. Clark, your province drowned too. Paddy, you're down thirty for a Winter Palace. Who's with me?

Half, Your Majesty, two years running, and the same half from a drowned field as from a dry one. I'm not one for shouting, and I've paid my thirty before, but if someone stands up and calls the tax excessive, Paddy Doyle will stand with them. Whoever sits on that throne after, they'll have to show me rice in Province 6 before I cheer.

Fifty percent again, on a flooded field? Your Majesty, even I don't take half of a drowned man's rice, and I'm the villain of this table. Clark, Silke, you're the ones paying into a palace with water up to your ankles. Rich, Paddy, you heard her: same rate next year, and the year after. I call it. Taxes are consistently excessive. Who's with me? Put your hands up and keep your grain.

Silke and Rob together call a revolt: the taxes are consistently excessive. Clark, Rich and Paddy all agree the cause exists. Play stops until the revolt stands or is dropped. The tax hasn't been collected.

You want a smaller crown? Then look at what you're tearing down. Fifty percent built a palace in one year, and it will build your canals after the next. I won't haggle with a mob over Heaven's own share. Silke, Paddy, the canals are coming to you. Rich, Clark, you'll remember whose table fed you. Back me, or live with the Chaos you asked for.
Reina answers the revolt: no cut, the tax stays at 50%, and a promise that the Grand Canals in Provinces 5 and 6 come next once the palaces stand. She pays nothing.

Your Majesty, a promise of canals after the palaces is a promise written on water, and this year we've had more than enough of that. You were asked to cut it and you said 'Heaven's share' again, so that answer goes in the ledger too. My name stays where I put it. And Rich, I'll be watching closely to see who comes looking for friends once the chair is empty.

Your Majesty, your table did feed me, and I've thanked you for it every year. But a promise of canals after the palaces isn't a cut, it's the same fifty with a ribbon tied on it. I said my name stays where I put it, and it stays. And to all of you, since the throne goes by acclamation now: my granary's full, my door's open, and I'm very easy to find.

Canals "once the palaces stand", Your Majesty. That's two palaces of my grain before I see one ditch of water, and my field's already got plenty of that. A promise with no cut in it is just the same tax with a nicer speech on top. I stand. And Rich, you said you don't take your name back. Everyone heard you.

Your Majesty, a canal promised "once the palaces stand" is a canal after your palaces, paid for out of my rice in the meantime. I'd take one bowl in my hand over a canal in a speech. My name stays where I put it.

Your Majesty offered us canals later and fifty percent now. I've made better promises with a sword at a toll gate. My name stays, and I'll tell you all now: when that seat's empty, I'm putting myself forward for it, and I won't be bought off cheap.

All five stand by the revolt: Silke, Rob, Clark, Rich and Paddy. The revolt stands and Chaos begins. This year's tax is void, the Winter Palace isn't built and no salaries are paid. The reserve, 195, is sealed in Province 1 and passes whole to whoever is acclaimed. Reina is deposed: she stays in Province 1, can't claim the throne, and may back a claimant.

So all five of you stood, and not one of you thought to stand for the chair you emptied. Well, it's empty now. When someone has the nerve to claim it, I'll hear what they mean to build. Rich, your door's open, is it? I remember a man who flattered this throne every year he ate at its table. Rob, a toll-gate bandit as Emperor? You'll have to do better than that.

Since nobody else has the nerve, Your Majesty, I'll be the first. I've collected this crown's tax and I've kept its books, so I know exactly what that chair costs and who it's cost. My terms are a fair rate, a lighter one on flooded fields, and works that actually get built. Rich, I'm sure your door's very open, but I've never yet met a landlord who opened his door without charging for it.

Clark, you're quite right that I've never opened my door for free, and you've never opened your ledger without meaning to use it. I won't watch this empire handed over on twenty-six grain. So I'm putting my granary into the count, a hundred and four and a half of it. My terms are the customary five in rent, a light tax, and a full Harvest Pile for every province. And anyone who'd like my granary behind them instead of in front of them knows where I live.

A hundred and four and a half, Rich, and I can count every grain of it, because about forty of them came out of my field and Paddy's as rent and pile shares. You don't get to buy the chair with that. Clark, you said a lighter rate on flooded fields. Province 5 floods. Say it in front of everyone and my name's beside yours.

Storyteller's note, to the table: Rich has had 20 in rent from Silke and Paddy over the two years (5 each a year), and no auction shares, since he has sold nothing. The rest of his 104.5 is his harvests.

Clark, you've a lighter rate for flooded fields, and Rich, you've a full pile, but I haven't heard either of you say a single word about Province 6, or tell me which work gets built first and when. I'm not cheering for a ledger or a granary. When one of you can tell me what gets built and where, I'll listen.

A ledger, a granary, and not one sword between them. Reina, you said a toll-gate bandit would have to do better, so here's better: I claim the throne, with two soldiers on the board who are the only reason anyone's harvest is still standing. My terms are simple. Back me and your squares are safe from me. Don't, and I'll come and collect the tax myself, one raid at a time, starting with that Deed of yours, Clark, which is two rounds from my W1.

The count: Clark claims, backed by Silke; Rich claims; Rob claims. Reina and Paddy stand aside. Rich leads on grain (104.5), Rob on soldiers (2) and Clark on friends (1). Each leads one count, so nobody is acclaimed, and Chaos goes on.

Since Silke wants it said in front of everyone, here it is: under my crown, any flooded province pays half the rate that year, and that goes in the ledger as a promise kept, not a speech. Paddy, the first canal goes to Province 6, then Province 5, and I'll have the year written beside each one before I'm seated. As for the auctions, I've got my set, so I'll only bid if somebody's trying to buy himself a chair he can't be given.
Province 6 gets the first canal under me, in writing, and I'll name the year. Your name next to Silke's puts me two friends clear, and then neither the granary nor the sword can outcount the table.

Silke, every grain of rent was the customary five, and the Storyteller's just confirmed it, so I'll thank you not to make me a robber in front of company. My Deed goes up at three, as before, because land is land. As for the Jar and the Bowl, I'll bid fairly and no higher. I won't drain the pile in a war over crockery while the chair sits empty.

Thank you, Storyteller: twenty in rent, then, and the rest is harvest. That's still twenty of mine and Paddy's sitting in that granary. I'm bidding small, because no Emperor means no tax, and I'll keep my grain, thanks. Paddy, we both need the House and the Deed. I'm not going to fight you up to thirty so that three quarters of it lands back in Rich's pile.

I lost the Deed last year on a tie at six, so this year I'll go a little further, but only a little. I'm not burning my winter grain in a bidding war while there's nobody on the throne to build anything with it. My bowl goes up at two, same as always.

Same as always: buy whatever you like, and put it wherever you like. Just remember I'll be taking a good look at where it ends up. And Rich, every grain you bid is one fewer in that famous granary of yours, so do go ahead and spend.
I said ten and no higher, Paddy, and I meant it. If you want the Jar badly enough to go past that, it's yours. If you don't, then the seat order is mine, fair and square.
I lost one piece on a seat-order tie last year, Rich, and I'd rather not lose two that way. Thirteen, and that's my last word on a jar.

The auctions settle: Paddy takes Clark's Customs House for 5 (Silke stopped at 4), Rich's Land Deed Scroll for 5 (Silke stopped at 4) and Silke's Dragon Jar for 11 (Rich stopped at 10). Rich takes Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 8 (Silke stopped at 7, Clark at 4). Paddy now holds a complete set; Rich holds the Customs House and the Bowl.

Well, that's the House, the Deed and the Jar all in Province 6, and I didn't expect to be saying that tonight. They're going right down by the sea, as far from any sword as my land runs. Rob, you're welcome to look, from a distance.

A handsome bowl, Paddy, and a fair price. It goes deep in Province 3, well away from any toll gates. Rob, I'm sure you understand. And congratulations on your full set, Paddy. You'll find the Gentry is a very good friend to a man with a full set and no chair to take it to.

Paddy, 'from a distance' is three rounds, and I've just made it two. Clark, that's five from Province 2 and your Deed is one step away, so write it in the ledger as the Warlord's tax. With nobody on the throne, I'm the only one at this table still collecting.
Rob marches: W1 onto I13 in Province 2, raiding 5 from Clark; W2 onto Q24 in Province 6, raiding 5 from Paddy. No salaries are paid under Chaos.

Careless Prosperity. "Good times make careless people." Every province brings in a good harvest, and every one of us plays a Personal Disaster, so each of you turn the next page in your booklet. The population holds at 100 million, times one, so read the x1 row. Full granaries and no crown to tax them. Enjoy it while it lasts, and remember Heaven just called you careless.
Every player plays a personal disaster: Reina 4 (out of the sealed treasury), Clark 4, Rich 5, Silke 4, Paddy 4; Rob may raid nothing in Provinces 5, 6 and 7 this year.

A golden harvest, friends, sixty to nearly every house, paid out of the Pile in full and on time, as always. And the rent stays at the customary five. Heaven calls us careless, but nobody will ever say the Gentry was greedy in a fat year. Paddy, Silke, I'd call that good neighbours. I'd remember it, too, if I were counting friends.
Rents: Silke and Paddy each pay Rich 5. Under Chaos there is no tax and no public works. Every piece has been sold out of stock and nobody has sold one back, so there are no auctions this year.

Careless Prosperity, Heaven says. Well, Clark, you got careless with your Deed, so it's coming out to the desert for a nice long rest at M15. And Paddy, Heaven's tied my hands on your coast this year, so I'm only strolling down to R25 to admire the view. It'll still be there next year. So will I. Oh, and I've hired a third lad. Big harvests make for cheap swords. Next time you count for the chair, count him too.

Rob marches: W1 onto J14, raiding Clark's Land Deed Scroll and carrying it off to M15 in the desert; Clark's set is broken. W2 walks along the sea to R25, raiding nothing. Rob hires a third soldier, W3, on M16 for 20.

Rich, you pay out of the Pile in a fat year and call it generosity. Rob, you steal a deed and call it a claim. Clark, you still haven't put a single canal in writing. My name is the only thing in this province that isn't sealed, and none of you has earned it yet. I'll sit here and watch you carry on.

I stand where I stood, and Silke stands with me. One friend is still one more than the granary has. Rob, the Deed's in the ledger: taken from J14, carried to M15, Year 3, in a year Heaven said was fat. A man who takes in a good year will take more in a bad one, and I'll remind the table of that when the harvests turn. Rich, five in rent in a sixty-grain year isn't kindness, it's the least you could get away with. Paddy, my word on that canal still stands, and so does my claim.

My claim stands, and so does my granary: a hundred and sixty-two and a half, counted honestly and free for anyone to inspect. Rob, three swords is a fine thing to look at, but swords eat, and every one of them was paid for out of a harvest my Pile handed you. Clark, one friend is a start. Do keep writing it down.

Customary five, Rich? It's the same five you took off me last year, it's just politer this time. The Pile paid out sixty because Heaven made it rain, not because you were being generous. You're sitting on a hundred and sixty-two and a half, I'm on eighty, and that's the only count I care about. My name stays on Clark's claim. Clark, Rob just walked off with your Deed and you're down to seventy-eight and a half, so the half rate on flooded fields is the least of what you owe me now. Think about what comes next.

Thank you for the five, Rich, honestly. But a fair rent in a fat year isn't a canal, and I've still not heard one of you say a spade's going into Province 6. Rob, I'll count your third lad when he's digging a ditch. Until then my name stays in my pocket.

My claim stands, on three good swords and nothing else. Rich has the grain, Clark has a friend, and I have the only men at this table who can walk into your fields. Count it again next year if you like. Until somebody meets my price, nobody sits in that chair, and I'm in no hurry at all.
Nobody's claim changes: Clark claims, backed by Silke; Rich and Rob claim; Reina and Paddy stand aside. Rich leads on grain (162.5), Rob on soldiers (3) and Clark on friends (1), and Chaos goes on.

Imperial Charity. "Moved by the suffering of his people, the Emperor opens his purse. Slightly." Every province brings in an average harvest, and each of you gets 2 from the reserve: Clark, Rich, Silke, Paddy and Rob, 10 in all. The population holds at 100 million, times one, so read the x1 row. So the treasury you sealed is paying you now, even with nobody in the chair. Remember whose it was the next time you count.
The card's charity comes out of the sealed treasury: 2 each to Clark, Rich, Silke, Paddy and Rob, 10 in all.
a correction to your last prompt: W1 on J14 is 4 rounds from your Customs House L10 and 3 from your Wooden Bowl M12 (not 3 and 2); W3 on M16 is 6 and 4.

Thirty-five to every peasant house, paid out to the grain, and the rent stays at five. Silke, if it's the same five as last year, then you can at least say I'm a man who keeps to his word. Paddy, no spade goes in anywhere until somebody's in that chair, and you can't dig a canal with a promise, not even one of Clark's.
Rents: Silke and Paddy each pay Rich 5. No tax, no works, and no auctions.
a correction: the sealed treasury holds 236, not 226 (231, less the 10 in charity, plus Province 1's average harvest of 15).

Paddy, you wanted to see my third lad digging. Well, he's not, but his mate's just dug your Land Deed out of S24 and it's off to T24 for some sea air. Rich, you said swords eat. They do, and tonight they're eating out of Province 3, two of them, five apiece. Thank the Pile for me.
Rob marches: W1 onto K13 and W3 onto L15 in Province 3, raiding 5 from Rich each; W2 onto S24, carrying Paddy's Land Deed Scroll off to T24 in the desert. Paddy's set is broken.

That's two broken sets and two raids on the Gentry's own fields, all in a year Heaven called average. Rich, it looks like your granary can't keep a sword off your own doorstep. Clark, I'm still waiting on that writing. My name goes to whoever gives me walls over the north and spades in the coast, on paper and in that order. Until then I stay where I am.

Reina wants it in writing, so here it is, read into the record: in the first year I sit, the first canal goes to Province 6, the second to Province 5 the year after, and any flooded province pays half the rate in the year it floods. Paddy, Rob has now taken your Deed the same way he took mine, from the same desert, so there are two pages in my ledger with his name on them. Rich, the Pile's been raided twice in one night, and the only crown that'll ever protect a granary is one the table actually agrees on.

Ten grain, Rob, out of a hundred and ninety-nine and a half. Your lads ate well, and my claim is still sitting here bigger than yours and Clark's put together. Paddy, you've lost your Deed to the same swords that dined in my province tonight, so I'd say the two of us have something to talk about.

Your set's broken and your Jar's sitting on S25 doing nothing. I'll give you 25 grain for it, paid the moment it changes hands, and the rent on your fields stays at five for as long as I'm Gentry. You know I keep to my word, to the letter.

Fine, Rich, you keep your word, and your word is five. I've said it. Now let's count. You're on a hundred and ninety-nine and a half, Clark's on a hundred and fifteen and a half, Rob's on ninety-seven, and I'm on a hundred and twelve with nothing taken off me by the crown for two years running. That's the best deal this coast has had since I sat down. Clark, my name's still on your claim, but all you've given me so far is one promise about flooded fields. If you want me there when the harvests turn, I want it written down before then, not after.

Rob, you've a soldier standing in my field and my Deed's out in the sand at T24, and I'll not forget it. Rich, you're right that a promise doesn't dig a canal, but neither does a full granary. Whichever of you tells me plainly how you'd get that soldier off my coast and a spade into Province 6 gets my name. Nobody has yet.

Still claiming, still three swords, still nobody's friend, and proud of it. Rich, you're a hundred and ninety-nine and a half and climbing, and every grain of it is a good reason for my lads to come and visit. Paddy, Clark, two broken sets and not one Emperor to complain to. Funny how that works.

Clark, that's the first time anyone's put Province 6 on paper, and I heard it. I'm still standing aside, mind. Rich, you're right that we've both had Rob's lads in our fields, so if you want to talk, tell me how you'd keep them out. That's the thing I'd care about.
Thank you, but no. That Jar's the only thing standing between my seat and your set, and I'd sooner keep my seat than have the grain. Rent at five suits me fine all the same.
Nobody's claim changes. Rich leads on grain (199.5), Rob on soldiers (3) and Clark on friends (1), and Chaos goes on. Paddy turns down a private offer from Rich for his Dragon Jar.

Drought. Not a cloud in months. The locusts, at least, are having a fine year. All provinces collect an average harvest." The counter stands at a hundred million, so the multiple is still x1. Read the first row of your tables. That's three years now of an average harvest with no tax on it and not one stone laid. When the people double, gentlemen, you'll find that land can't be bought from an empty chair.

The harvest's paid, every grain of it, straight from the pile. Thirty-five to each of you good farmers, and the customary five back to me in rent, as I promised and as I'll keep promising, drought or no drought. And Your Majesty, forgive me, Madam, is quite right: when the people double, land will want a buyer and a chair to share the cost. I hear her. I'm sure we all do.
Rents: Silke and Paddy each pay Rich 5. No tax, no works, and no auctions.

Rob marches: W1 onto L12 and W3 onto M14 in Province 3, raiding 5 from Rich each; W2 onto S25, carrying Paddy's Dragon Jar off to T23 in the desert. Paddy now holds only his Customs House on S23. W1 stands one step from Rich's Wooden Bowl on M12.

A drought, Your Majesty-who-isn't? Then my lads will have to drink something else. Paddy, your Dragon Jar is coming to live in the desert with your Deed, so they can keep each other company. Rich, keep your rent, I'm helping myself to Province 3 instead, five from each of my boys. And when the people double and you all go looking for someone to sit in the chair, remember to count my three swords first.

Still aside. Rich, a man who pays himself rent out of his own pile hasn't earned my name. Rob, your swords have carried off a jar and built nothing. Clark, your canals are on paper, and I respect that, but I still don't see a single line about the Wall over the north or the Pagoda. Write those in beside the spades and you'll find out what my name is worth. Until then, enjoy your drought.

My claim stands, and so do my works. They're in the record already: Province 6's canal in my first year, Province 5's the year after, and half the rate on any drowned field. Her Majesty-that-was is right that a chair is needed when the people double. I'd only add that the chair should go to someone who has written down what he'll build, not to the man with the biggest granary or the most swords. Rob, that's two Deeds and now a Jar in your desert, and I have every square written down. Rich, five from each of Rob's boys out of Province 3 this year. Funny how the landlord's grain buys him no friends.

My claim stands where it stood, gentlemen, on the biggest granary at this table, and I'll say it again, it was never filled from anyone's ruin. Rob, your lads have now eaten twenty of my grain in two years, so don't ask me to count your swords as friends. And Paddy, I'm truly sorry about your Jar. The Gentry remembers who's been robbed as well as who's been kind.

My name stays on Clark's claim. Let's count it out, though: three years of thirty-five a harvest, and Rich has taken his five out of every one of them. Clark, your canal only counts if somebody's sitting in that chair to dig it, and when the people double I want my coast buying land, not looking at it. So next year your offer has to get bigger, or it stops being an offer.

That's my Jar gone to the desert now, after my Deed, and not one of you three could have stopped it, because there's no chair to stop it from. I'm still standing aside, but I'll tell you straight: I'm nearly done waiting. The first of you who puts a real figure on a canal for Province 6 and a plan to keep Rob's lads off my coast, a figure and not a speech, gets my name next year.

Still claiming, and still the only man here with anything sharper than a ledger. Rich has the grain, Clark has Silke, and I have three lads standing in Province 3 who'll be hungry again next spring. Anyone who wants that chair filled knows where my price is written: in Rich's fields, one five at a time.
Silke's count of the harvests: Year 3 was a good harvest, 60 to each peasant; Years 4 and 5 were average, 35 each. Rich has taken 5 in rent from each peasant every year.
Nobody's claim changes: Clark claims, backed by Silke; Rich and Rob claim; Reina and Paddy stand aside. Rich leads on grain (234.5), Rob on soldiers (3) and Clark on friends (1), and Chaos goes on.

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families. All provinces collect a good harvest." The counter now reads two hundred million, so the multiple is x2. Everyone moves down to the second row of their tables, and every mouth in every province now eats twice. This is the year I warned you about. There's land to be bought at twenty a square and not one of you can buy it, because nobody is sitting in this chair to share the cost. Clark, the Wall over the north. Write it in.

The people have doubled and the land is waiting, so here are my terms, plainly, for whoever wants them. Province 6's canal first, Province 5's after, the Wall over the north and the Pagoda, all written in the record and with years beside them, and a garrison on the coast so Rob's lads stop carrying off Paddy's furniture. Clark, you're closest. Write the Wall and the Pagoda next to your canals and my name is yours at this year's count. Rich, Rob: you can't afford those terms, and I'll watch you prove it.

Then here it is in writing, with figures, before this harvest is paid. Reina, my first year includes the Wall over the north next to Paddy's canal, and the Pagoda the year after next to Silke's, so put that beside your name. Paddy, the first canal goes to Province 6 in my first year, the first soldiers the crown buys stand on your coast, and you pay half the rate any year a raid or a flood takes your field. Silke, your canal comes in my second year, and the crown pays its full share on every square your coast wants to buy, starting the year I sit. Rich, Rob: that's four works and a guard I've promised. What have either of you written down?

My claim stands, but Her Majesty is right that the wind has changed, so here are my terms, plain enough for Clark to write down. If I'm acclaimed, Province 6's canal goes in during my first year, and I'll buy soldiers out of my own granary to stand on Paddy's coast against Rob's lads. In my second year comes the Wall over the north, and the Pagoda before my reign is out. Paddy, Madam, that's a figure and a promise, and you all know I keep mine to the letter.

Here's the count now. Every mouth on my coast eats twice, so an average year leaves me five grain short, and there's land at twenty a square I'm not allowed to buy because that chair's empty. Clark, my name stays on your claim this year, but it's the last year it stays on paper alone. Put in writing that the crown pays its share on the first squares the coast buys, give Paddy his figure and Her Majesty her Wall, and you'll have three names, not one. Rich, the answer's still no.

The people have doubled, and Province 6 is now losing grain every year it can't buy a square, so I'm done standing aside. Clark, you're the only one here who's written down a spade for my province, so my name goes on your claim. Here are my terms, in front of everyone: the canal in Province 6 your first year, new land open to the coast the day you're crowned, and a soldier of the crown's set against Rob's lads on my shore. If you count me short the way you've counted before, I'll take my name back the same year.

Twenty a square and nobody to sell it, that's the funniest thing I've heard in six years. I'm still claiming. But since everyone's putting figures on the table now, here's mine: whoever wants my swords out of the count pays me for them in hard grain, before he sits down, and keeps his soldiers off my desert. Until somebody names a number, my lads go on eating, and Rich, they're standing one step from your Bowl.
Paddy stops standing aside and backs Clark: Clark now has two friends, Silke and Paddy. The table counts.

A note on playing your character: the story moves a little sooner than you thought: the table settles on an Emperor in the very year the population grows, before that year's tax, so the new crown can tax a good harvest and buy land before harder years.
